energy_regime.quote: It was conceived to study proton-proton (and lead-lead) collisions at a centre-of-mass energy of 14 TeV (5.5 TeV nucleon-nucleon) and at luminosities up to 10^34 cm^-2 s^-1 (10^27 cm^-2 s^-1).
energy_regime.value: Proton-proton (and heavy-ion) collisions at TeV centre-of-mass energies: designed for 14 TeV, 13.6 TeV delivered in LHC Run 3

facility_roles.quote: Point 5 of the LHC, in Cessy, is home to the CMS detector, which weighs in at 12 500 tonnes (twice the weight of the Eiffel Tower).

intervals.label: Letter of Intent
intervals.note: Start: the CMS Letter of Intent was submitted to the LHCC on 1 October 1992 (also the date_proposed field of the INSPIRE experiment record). The end is derived from the approval date.
intervals.quote: This 103 pages long document was submitted to the LHC Committee on the 1st of October 1992. This is considered the 'birth day' of CMS.

intervals.label: Approved
intervals.note: Approval date from the INSPIRE experiment record. CMS's own history timeline instead labels 1993 'CMS project approved' — see worklog conflict C1. The end is derived from the start of construction at Point 5.

intervals.label: Construction
intervals.note: Excavation of the Point 5 caverns began in 1998; the last detector element was lowered on 22 January 2008.
intervals.quote: Between 1998 and 2005 a total of almost 250,000 m3 of soil and rock was excavated

intervals.label: Detector lowering
intervals.quote: The first lowering took place in November 2006, and the last on 22 January 2008.

intervals.label: First collisions
intervals.note: The LHC first collided 450 GeV beams (900 GeV centre of mass) on 23 November 2009, the date_started field of the INSPIRE experiment record; the first sustained collision period began on 6 December 2009. The end date is derived as the day before the first 7 TeV physics collisions.
intervals.quote: On 23rd November the LHC collided 450 GeV beams of protons for the first time...The first real period of collisions started on 6th December.

intervals.label: LHC Run 1
intervals.note: 7 TeV (2010–2011) and 8 TeV (2012) proton-proton collisions, plus heavy-ion running.
intervals.quote: Beams collided at 7 TeV in the LHC at 13:06 CEST, marking the start of the LHC research programme.

intervals.label: Long Shutdown 1
intervals.note: CMS consolidation: pixel detector repairs and Phase-1 pilot modules, HCAL photodetector replacement, additional muon chambers, trigger and DAQ work. End year derived from the start of Run 2.
intervals.quote: In the early hours of 14 February 2013, the first period of running for the Large Hadron Collider came to an end.

intervals.label: LHC Run 2
intervals.note: CERN states Run 2 ended on 3 December 2018 'after three fantastic years'. The exact 2015 restart date could not be confirmed from a source fetched in this session, so the start is recorded at year precision.
intervals.quote: On 3 December, the LHC's second run came to an end after three fantastic years.

intervals.label: Long Shutdown 2 (Phase-1 upgrades)
intervals.note: Interval between the end of Run 2 and the start of Run 3, during which CMS completed its Phase-1 upgrade programme. Both bounds are the adjacent run boundaries rather than a shutdown announcement.

intervals.label: LHC Run 3
intervals.note: 13.6 TeV proton-proton collisions from 5 July 2022. End at month precision: CERN announced on 29 June 2026 that, following its final physics run, the accelerator had been switched off.
intervals.quote: Yesterday, 5th of July 2022, the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN delivered proton-proton collisions ... at the energy of 13.6 trillion electron volts (TeV) for the first time

end.note: HiLumi LHC scheduled to begin operation in 2030

intervals.label: Long Shutdown 3 — Phase-2 upgrade
intervals.note: Phase-2 upgrade of CMS for the HL-LHC: new all-silicon tracker, new high-granularity endcap calorimeter, MIP timing detector, muon system extensions and a new trigger/DAQ. The end date is from CERN’s schedule and is marked planned.
intervals.quote: As of mid-2026, the accelerator complex and experimental facilities at CERN are undergoing major maintenance and upgrade work. This phase, known as 'Long Shutdown 3' or 'LS3', is expected to last up to four years.

physics_goals.value: Search for and characterise the Higgs boson

summary.plain: One of the two big general-purpose experiments at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Thousands of scientists use it to photograph the debris of proton collisions 40 million times a second. In 2012 it was one of the two experiments that found the Higgs boson.
summary.technical: General-purpose pp and heavy-ion collider experiment at LHC Point 5 (Cessy, France). CMS uses a 12 500 t, 21.6 m × 14.6 m detector built around a 3.8 T solenoid to study electroweak symmetry breaking, Higgs boson properties, top-quark and QCD physics, flavour physics, heavy-ion collisions and direct searches for physics beyond the standard model.

unique_capabilities.quote: the largest superconducting magnet ever built
unique_capabilities.value: A 3.8 T superconducting solenoid — the largest superconducting magnet ever built — whose iron return yoke doubles as the absorber of the muon system

unique_capabilities.quote: The concept of building large objects on the surface and transferring them completed to the underground area was the clear way to go
unique_capabilities.value: Built in fifteen sections in a surface hall and lowered complete into the cavern 100 m below, a first for a collider detector
